t: Find the Maximum Divisibility Score — Brute Force Counting
o: For each divisor, count how many nums it divides; return the divisor with the highest count, ties broken by smallest value. Constraints (both arrays ≤ 1000) sanction the O(N·D) double loop — about 10^6 modulo operations.
k: Nothing beats direct enumeration here; the constraint product is tiny.
Tie-breaking by smaller divisor means strict '>' comparison when updating the best.

a.i: Compute each score with an inner loop over nums, keeping (bestScore, bestDivisor) updated with strict improvement so earlier/smaller divisors win ties naturally when iterating in order — but since divisors aren't sorted, compare (score, -divisor) lexicographically or require score > best || (score == best && d < bestD).
s: For each d in divisors: cnt = #{x in nums : x % d == 0}.
Update if cnt > best, or cnt == best and d < bestD.
a.t: O(N·D) — every (num, divisor) pair checked once, ≤ 10^6 operations.

w: One approach suffices; if asked to optimize, deduplicate divisors first or precompute nothing helps asymptotically since divisibility is pairwise. Pitfalls: using '>=' instead of '>' breaks the tie-break toward larger divisors seen later; initializing bestD incorrectly. Follow-up: many queries against a fixed nums array (precompute divisor-count maps via smallest-prime-factor factorization).
